title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
description: Brute force to optimized: collecting every value via a full inorder traversal versus an iterative inorder traversal that stops the moment the kth value is found.

content.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given the root of a binary search tree, and an integer k, return the kth smallest value among all the values in the tree (1-indexed).

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["The tree is a BST, and values are needed in sorted order","Inorder traversal, which visits a BST's values in strictly increasing order"],["Only the kth value is needed, not the full sorted list","An iterative, stack-based inorder traversal that can stop early, the moment the kth value is reached"]]}

blocks.text: Given a BST, find the value that would appear at position k if every value in the tree were listed out in increasing order.

blocks.title: Analogy: Reading Name Tags Off a Sorted Family Tree
blocks.text: Picture a binary search tree as a family tree drawn so that visiting left child, node, then right child always reads names off in alphabetical order. The kth smallest value is simply the kth name encountered while reading it that way.

blocks.caption: An inorder traversal (left, node, right) visits a BST's values in sorted order

blocks.text: The sorted order of values is 1, 2, 3, 4; the 1st smallest is 1.
The 3rd smallest, in sorted order 1, 2, 3, 4, is 3.
Before collecting and sorting every value in the tree, notice that a BST's inorder traversal already visits values in sorted order for free, no sorting needed.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: In a binary search tree, every node's left subtree holds smaller values and its right subtree holds larger values, so visiting left, then the node, then right, always produces values in increasing order.

Observation 2: Since the traversal is already sorted, the kth value visited during an inorder traversal IS the kth smallest value, no separate sort needed.

Observation 3: An iterative inorder traversal using an explicit stack can be paused at any point, letting the traversal stop the very moment the kth node is reached.

Observation 4: This avoids visiting or storing any values beyond the kth one.
This leads to an iterative, stack-based inorder traversal that returns as soon as it has visited exactly k nodes.
Perform a full inorder traversal, collecting every value into a list, then return the element at position k minus 1.

items: Traverse the tree inorder (left, node, right), appending every visited value to a list.
Return the value at index k minus 1 in that list.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: collect every value via inorder traversal, then index into the list

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The full inorder traversal always runs to completion, even when k is small and the answer would be found early.
Every value is stored, using O(n) space regardless of how small k is.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), visiting every node regardless of k.
Space: O(n), storing every value.
Limitation: when k is much smaller than the total number of nodes, the traversal still visits and stores every remaining value after the answer has already been found.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why collecting every value is unnecessary: the inorder traversal visits values in increasing order one at a time, so the kth one can be recognized the moment it is visited, without needing the rest.

How to pause a traversal mid-way: an iterative inorder traversal using an explicit stack, rather than recursion, can be stopped and its result returned as soon as the kth node is popped.

The core idea: push left children onto a stack, pop and count each visited node, and return as soon as the count reaches k.

Use an explicit stack to simulate inorder traversal: repeatedly push left children until reaching a leaf, then pop a node, count it, and move to its right child, pushing its left children, and so on. Return the value the moment the count reaches k.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Stack pushes","Popped (visit order)","Count"],"rows":[["Push left spine from 3","3, 1","-","0"],["Pop 1, no right child","-","1","1"],["Pop 3, push left spine of right child (4, no left)","4","3","2"],["Pop 4","-","4","3 (matches k, return 4)"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: iterative inorder with an explicit stack, stopping early at the kth node

blocks.text: An iterative inorder traversal visits nodes in exactly the same sorted order as the recursive version, but does so one step at a time using an explicit stack, allowing the traversal to be paused and its result returned immediately once the kth node has been popped, without ever visiting or storing the remaining nodes.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(h plus k), where h is the tree's height, in the worst case O(n) if k is close to n, but often much faster for small k.
Space: O(h), the stack only ever holds one root-to-leaf path's worth of nodes.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Brute force (collect all values, then index)","O(n)","O(n)","Correct, but always does full work regardless of k."],["Optimized (iterative inorder, stop early)","O(h + k)","O(h)","The expected answer, can stop far earlier when k is small."]]}

blocks.text: The key insight is that a BST's inorder traversal already produces sorted order for free; the only additional idea needed is making that traversal iterative so it can stop early the moment the kth value is found.

items: Using a recursive inorder traversal that cannot easily stop early without extra bookkeeping (like a counter passed by reference).
Off-by-one errors between a 1-indexed k and a 0-indexed count of nodes visited.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["k equals the total number of nodes","Returns the maximum value in the tree, the last one visited."],["A tree with a single node","k must be 1, and the answer is that node's value."]]}

blocks.text: Stating clearly why inorder traversal produces sorted order in a BST specifically (not in a general binary tree) is the foundational fact this solution rests on.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "can you avoid visiting the whole tree", think: an iterative inorder traversal with an explicit stack can stop the instant the kth node is popped.

items: How would you handle the BST being modified (insertions or deletions) frequently, with many kth-smallest queries in between?
How would this change for finding the kth LARGEST value instead?
Any "kth smallest/largest via sorted traversal" problem on a BST.
The general iterative inorder traversal technique, reusable across many tree problems needing early termination.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n) time and O(n) space. The optimized iterative inorder traversal runs in O(h plus k) time and O(h) space.

items: Pattern: iterative inorder traversal with early termination.
Core Idea: a BST's inorder traversal visits values in sorted order for free; stop as soon as the kth value is popped from an explicit stack.
Time: O(n) for the brute force, O(h plus k) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n) for the brute force, O(h) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: no sorting is ever needed, a BST's structure already guarantees sorted order via inorder traversal.
Interview Difficulty: straightforward once the BST-inorder-sorted-order fact is recognized.
One line memory trick: inorder traversal is already sorted; stop at the kth pop.
